question_text: A company needs to document the capabilities, limitations, intended uses, and biases of the FM they have fine-tuned to satisfy internal governance and potential regulatory review. Which AWS mechanism supports this?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail logs
Amazon SageMaker AI programmatic model cards
Amazon Inspector vulnerability reports
AWS Config configuration history

explanation: Skill 3.3.1 cites SageMaker AI for developing programmatic model cards. Model cards are structured documents that record a model's intended use, performance metrics, fairness evaluation, limitations, and training data provenance — a governance and compliance artefact. CloudTrail logs API calls, not model documentation. Inspector reports security vulnerabilities. Config records resource configuration changes — not model metadata.
source_topic: SageMaker model cards, AI governance

question_text: An organisation must be able to trace which data sources contributed to any specific FM-generated output for regulatory audit purposes. Which service provides automated data lineage tracking?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch
AWS Glue — using the Glue Data Catalog to register data sources and track lineage
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Athena

explanation: Skill 3.3.2 cites AWS Glue Data Catalog to register data sources and metadata tagging for source attribution in FM-generated content, plus CloudTrail for audit logging. AWS Glue tracks data origins, transformations, and target destinations — enabling data lineage chains. CloudWatch monitors metrics and logs. Kinesis Firehose is a streaming data delivery service. Athena runs SQL queries — neither natively provides lineage tracking.
source_topic: AWS Glue Data Catalog, data lineage, FM governance

question_text: A financial services company must continuously monitor its GenAI application for model drift, policy violations, and ensure AI outputs comply with regulatory requirements — with automated alerting when violations are detected. Which approach best addresses this?

options.text: Run monthly manual audits of FM outputs
Implement automated monitoring using CloudWatch with custom metrics for bias drift, policy violations, and token-level response analysis; configure alarms and SNS notifications for violations
Store all FM outputs in S3 and review them quarterly
Use Amazon Inspector to scan FM outputs for compliance violations

explanation: Skill 3.3.4 describes automated detection for misuse, drift, and policy violations; bias drift monitoring; and automated alerting and remediation workflows. CloudWatch custom metrics can track hallucination rates, topic violation counts, and response quality scores; alarms with SNS notifications trigger immediate alerts. Monthly manual audits detect violations late. Quarterly S3 review is too infrequent. Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities — not FM semantic compliance.
source_topic: CloudWatch, compliance monitoring, bias drift, FM governance

question_text: An enterprise must maintain an immutable audit trail of who invoked which FM, when, and with what parameters for a 7-year retention period. Which AWS service provides this?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch Logs
AWS CloudTrail
Amazon S3 server access logging
Amazon VPC Flow Logs

explanation: Skill 3.3.2 cites CloudTrail for audit logging of FM usage. CloudTrail records every Bedrock API call with caller identity, timestamp, source IP, and request parameters — creating an immutable audit log. CloudTrail logs can be stored in S3 with Object Lock for compliance. CloudWatch Logs capture application logs but lack the IAM-identity audit depth of CloudTrail. S3 server access logs record S3 operations, not Bedrock API calls. VPC Flow Logs capture network traffic metadata — not API-level identity audit.
source_topic: AWS CloudTrail, audit logging, FM governance

question_text: A company wants a comprehensive AI governance framework that aligns FM deployments with organisational policies, regulatory requirements, and responsible AI principles. Which elements are ESSENTIAL components of such a framework? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Documented policies covering FM selection criteria, approved use cases, and prohibited applications
A bias drift monitoring system with regular fairness evaluations
Maximising model parameter count across all deployed FMs
Restricting all access to a single FM to reduce complexity
Deploying FMs only in AWS regions with the lowest latency

explanation: Skill 3.3.3 describes comprehensive governance frameworks aligned with policies, regulatory requirements, and responsible AI principles. Skill 3.3.4 adds bias drift monitoring and automated governance controls. (A) documented policies establish guardrails for FM selection and usage; (B) bias drift monitoring catches fairness degradation over time. Parameter count is an engineering metric, not a governance component. Restricting to a single FM limits capability without governance benefit. Region selection is an operational decision, not a governance framework element.
source_topic: Responsible AI governance, bias monitoring, policy

topic: S3 Object Lock for 7-year immutable compliance logging
question_text: A regulated insurance company must retain all FM model invocation logs (full prompt and response payloads) for 7 years. The logs must be tamper-proof — not modifiable or deletable by anyone, including AWS account administrators. Which storage configuration achieves this?

options.text: Store logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs with a 7-year retention policy
Store logs in Amazon S3 with Object Lock in Compliance mode and a 7-year retention period
Store logs in DynamoDB with IAM policies preventing deletion
Enable CloudTrail data events for Bedrock with a 7-year S3 lifecycle policy

explanation: Skill 3.3.4 describes immutable audit logging for regulatory readiness. S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode is the highest level of immutability: once set, no principal — not even the AWS root account — can delete or overwrite objects before the retention period expires. This is the WORM (Write Once Read Many) standard required by financial regulations (SEC/FINRA). CloudWatch Logs retention policies define when logs are purged — not immutable. IAM policies can be overridden by account administrators. CloudTrail captures API metadata (who called the API, when) — not the full prompt/response payload that Bedrock Model Invocation Logging provides.
source_topic: S3 Object Lock Compliance mode, WORM, compliance logging

question_text: A manufacturing company rolls out an AI governance policy requiring every Bedrock InvokeModel and Converse API call to include a guardrail. Developers sometimes forget to attach a guardrail ID in their code. What is the MOST operationally efficient way to enforce this at the infrastructure level?

options.text: Deploy a Lambda proxy that validates guardrail presence before forwarding requests to Bedrock
Store the guardrail ID in Parameter Store and write a code review checklist
Configure IAM policies with the bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition key on every IAM role that calls Bedrock — requests without a guardrail ID are denied at the AWS IAM layer
Train developers on the importance of guardrails in quarterly workshops

explanation: Skill 3.3.3 describes organisational governance systems for consistent oversight. The IAM condition key `bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier` enforces guardrail attachment at the infrastructure level: any API call that omits the guardrail ID is immediately rejected with AccessDenied — no custom code required. This is zero-maintenance once configured. A Lambda proxy (A) introduces latency, adds a failure point, and requires ongoing maintenance — poor operational efficiency. Parameter Store + code review (B) relies on humans, is error-prone. Training (D) cannot enforce compliance technically.
source_topic: IAM condition key bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier, AI governance

question_text: A financial services firm uses Amazon Bedrock for a multimodal application that processes images alongside text. A compliance audit requires that both the input images and the model responses are logged and stored for 7 years. What is the CORRECT approach?

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging with full request and response capture, storing logs in an S3 bucket with a lifecycle policy that retains objects for 7 years
Log only the text portions; images cannot be captured by invocation logging
Store logs solely in CloudWatch Logs with default 90-day retention
Retain the CloudTrail logs, which capture image payloads automatically

explanation: Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logging can capture full request payloads (including images) and responses when enabled, and logs can be directed to S3 with an appropriate retention lifecycle policy. Invocation logging does support multimodal content — it is not limited to text only. CloudWatch Logs has a maximum configurable retention that may not cover 7 years, and default retention is 90 days. CloudTrail records API control-plane events but does not capture inference payload bodies.
source_topic: Bedrock Model Invocation Logging, multimodal audit, compliance retention

question_text: A compliance officer asks: 'How can we prove which IAM user or role invoked a specific Amazon Bedrock model, on what date, and from which IP address?' Which AWS service provides this immutable audit trail?

options.text: Amazon CloudWatch Metrics — tracks invocation counts per model
Amazon Bedrock Model Invocation Logs — captures full prompt and response content
AWS CloudTrail — records who called which API, when, and from where
AWS Config — tracks configuration changes to Bedrock resources

explanation: AWS CloudTrail is the definitive audit service recording all AWS API calls: identity (who — IAM user/role/service), timestamp (when), source IP (where), service (what API — bedrock:InvokeModel), and target resource. This is the immutable compliance audit trail. CloudWatch Metrics shows aggregate counts, not individual identities. Bedrock Invocation Logs capture prompt/response CONTENT — useful for content audit but not the primary identity/access audit tool. Config tracks resource configurations, not runtime API calls.
source_topic: CloudTrail for identity-based Bedrock API audit trail

question_text: A data governance team asks: 'Which S3 bucket did our RAG knowledge base training data originate from, which Glue ETL job processed it, and which Bedrock Knowledge Base ingested it?' Which AWS service provides this data provenance trail?

options.text: AWS CloudTrail — API call audit trail
Amazon CloudWatch — metrics and logs monitoring
AWS Glue Data Catalog — stores metadata, schema, and lineage for data assets
Amazon Macie — sensitive data discovery

explanation: AWS Glue Data Catalog is the metadata repository that tracks data lineage — recording where data came from (source S3 buckets), what transformations were applied (Glue ETL jobs), and where it went (downstream consumers like Bedrock Knowledge Bases). This answers 'what data exists and where did it come from?' CloudTrail answers 'who called which API?' CloudWatch is monitoring. Macie discovers PII.
source_topic: AWS Glue Data Catalog for data lineage in GenAI pipelines

question_text: A company deploys a custom fine-tuned SageMaker model to production. The legal team requires documentation of the model's purpose, training data used, known limitations, bias assessment results, and intended use cases — stored as a formal artifact alongside the model. Which SageMaker feature provides this?

options.text: SageMaker Experiments — tracks training run parameters and metrics
SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking — records artifact relationships
SageMaker Model Cards — structured documentation of model purpose, limitations, and responsible AI metadata
SageMaker Pipelines — defines the training workflow

explanation: SageMaker Model Cards are purpose-built for documenting ML models in a standardised format: intended use, training data, performance metrics, known limitations, ethical considerations, and bias assessment results. This formal artefact can be stored in Model Registry and shared with stakeholders. Experiments tracks training metrics. ML Lineage Tracking records artifact relationships. Pipelines defines the workflow — none of these produce the human-readable governance documentation that Model Cards provide.
source_topic: SageMaker Model Cards for responsible AI documentation

question_text: A healthcare company using Amazon Bedrock needs to obtain AWS's SOC 2 Type II report and HIPAA Business Associate Agreement (BAA) to satisfy their compliance auditor. Where should they access these documents?

options.text: AWS Security Hub — provides security posture findings
AWS Artifact — self-service portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements
Amazon Macie — data privacy and compliance service
AWS Config — resource configuration compliance tool

explanation: AWS Artifact is the self-service portal providing on-demand access to AWS compliance documentation: SOC 1/2/3 reports, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, HIPAA BAA, GDPR DPA, FedRAMP, and 100+ other compliance artefacts. Security Hub monitors security posture. Macie discovers sensitive data. Config checks resource configurations. None of these provide the downloadable compliance certification documents that AWS Artifact provides.
source_topic: AWS Artifact for SOC/HIPAA/PCI compliance documentation

question_text: A platform team wants automatic detection and alerting when any Bedrock Guardrail configuration is modified (e.g., a safety threshold is lowered). Which combination of services provides this continuous governance monitoring?

options.text: Amazon Macie scheduled scans of the Guardrail S3 artefact
AWS CloudTrail (record CreateGuardrail/UpdateGuardrail API events) + Amazon EventBridge rule (pattern match on Bedrock Guardrail events) + SNS notification
SageMaker Model Monitor watching Guardrail drift
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with self-monitoring capability

explanation: CloudTrail records all management API events including UpdateGuardrail — capturing who changed what and when. EventBridge can match CloudTrail events matching bedrock:UpdateGuardrail and trigger an SNS notification to alert the security team. This provides real-time automated governance alerting on configuration changes. Macie scans data, not API events. Model Monitor watches ML endpoint behaviour, not Guardrail configs. Guardrails don't self-monitor.
source_topic: CloudTrail + EventBridge + SNS for Guardrail change alerting

question_text: A company wants to tag all AWS resources used in their GenAI application with metadata including Project, Owner, DataClassification, and ComplianceScheme (GDPR/HIPAA). What is the PRIMARY benefit of this tagging strategy?

options.text: Tags encrypt the resource data automatically
Tags enable cost allocation, compliance tracking, access control via ABAC, and automated remediation based on metadata
Tags replace IAM policies for access control
Tags increase the performance of Bedrock models

explanation: Resource tagging enables: (1) cost allocation and chargeback by project/owner in Cost Explorer, (2) compliance reporting by filtering resources by ComplianceScheme, (3) attribute-based access control (ABAC) via IAM tag conditions, and (4) automated remediation (AWS Config rules can detect untagged resources and trigger auto-remediation). Tags don't provide encryption, don't replace IAM, and don't affect model performance.
source_topic: Resource tagging for GenAI governance and cost allocation

topic: NIST AI RMF as governance framework
question_text: A US federal agency deploying a Bedrock-based document classification system needs to follow official AI risk management standards for US government information systems. Which framework should guide their AI governance approach?

options.text: PCI-DSS — Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
HIPAA — Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)
FedRAMP — for cloud service authorisation only

explanation: NIST AI RMF is the US federal standard for managing AI risks in government information systems. It provides a structured framework for AI trustworthiness across the dimensions of governance, mapping, measurement, and management. PCI-DSS covers payment card security. HIPAA governs health data privacy. FedRAMP authorises cloud services for federal use but doesn't provide comprehensive AI risk guidance. NIST AI RMF (combined with NIST SP 800-series) is the correct answer.
source_topic: NIST AI RMF for US federal AI governance

question_text: A DevOps team wants to automatically reject deployment pipeline runs where Bedrock prompt templates in the source repository contain phrases that violate the company's AI policy (e.g., they instruct the model to bypass safety controls). Where in the CI/CD pipeline should this check be added?

options.text: After production deployment — scan logs for policy violations post-deployment
As a CodeBuild step in the CodePipeline before deployment — scan prompt template files for policy violations and fail the pipeline on violations
Use Bedrock Guardrails to block the violating prompts at runtime
Use Amazon Macie to scan the prompt repository

explanation: Compliance checks should be integrated as early as possible (shift-left). Adding a CodeBuild step to scan prompt templates for policy violations before deployment fails the pipeline if violations are detected — preventing non-compliant prompts from ever reaching production. Post-deployment scanning (A) is too late. Guardrails (C) is a runtime control, not a design-time policy gate. Macie discovers PII in S3, not policy violations in code/prompt files.
source_topic: Shift-left: CodePipeline + CodeBuild for prompt compliance scanning

question_text: A company processes both text and image inputs through Amazon Bedrock multimodal models. Their compliance team requires that ALL model invocations (including image inputs and text responses) be logged for a 3-year audit period. How should they configure this?

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail data events for Bedrock — it logs all modalities including images
Enable Bedrock Model Invocation Logging via PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration to an S3 bucket, which captures all input modalities and responses
Add logging code in every Lambda function that calls Bedrock
Use Amazon Transcribe to log audio inputs and Amazon Textract to log image inputs separately

explanation: Bedrock Model Invocation Logging (enabled via PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration) is the purpose-built feature that captures complete invocation records — including text and image inputs across all modalities, responses, model IDs, timestamps, and metadata — to S3 or CloudWatch Logs. CloudTrail records API management events (metadata) but NOT the full request/response body including image data. Per-Lambda manual logging is error-prone and incomplete. Transcribe/Textract are separate processing services.
source_topic: Bedrock Model Invocation Logging for multimodal audit

question_text: A security operations team wants to: (1) find ALL API management calls made to Bedrock (CreateKnowledgeBase, UpdateGuardrail, etc.) — who did it and when, (2) retrieve the actual prompts and responses from production model calls for content review, (3) trace request latency from API Gateway through Lambda to Bedrock. Which THREE services map to these requirements?

options.text: (1) AWS CloudTrail — records all management API calls with identity and timestamp
(2) Bedrock Model Invocation Logs — captures full prompt and response content
(3) AWS X-Ray — distributed tracing across API Gateway, Lambda, and Bedrock
(1) Amazon CloudWatch Metrics — tracks API call counts per operation
(3) AWS CloudTrail — traces request latency per service

explanation: (1) CloudTrail is the definitive tool for management API audit: who called CreateKnowledgeBase/UpdateGuardrail and when. (2) Bedrock Model Invocation Logs (via S3/CloudWatch Logs) capture the actual prompt and response content of every model call. (3) AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing showing per-segment latency across the entire request path (API Gateway → Lambda → Bedrock). CloudWatch Metrics (D) shows aggregate counts, not per-call identities. CloudTrail (E) doesn't measure latency.
source_topic: CloudTrail vs Invocation Logs vs X-Ray — three Bedrock log types

question_text: A GenAI application must log every model interaction with the following fields: user_id, session_id, prompt_version, model_id, tokens_used, response_time_ms, and a truncated response summary. This is needed for both cost attribution and compliance. What is the BEST storage design for these structured logs?

options.text: Write structured JSON logs to CloudWatch Logs; use Logs Insights for queries and export to S3 for long-term retention
Write to DynamoDB — NoSQL is ideal for log storage
Write to Amazon RDS — relational structure is required for compliance
Use Amazon Kinesis to stream logs and discard after processing

explanation: CloudWatch Logs stores structured JSON logs from Lambda, supports Logs Insights for real-time queries (cost attribution, compliance checks), and can be exported to S3 for long-term Glacier archival. This provides the full cost attribution + compliance retention pipeline. DynamoDB is expensive for high-volume write-heavy log storage. RDS adds schema management overhead for a log store. Kinesis + discard loses data needed for compliance.
source_topic: Structured FM interaction logging to CloudWatch + S3 export

question_text: A company monitors their Bedrock Guardrails and wants to be automatically alerted when the number of blocked requests in a 5-minute window exceeds 100 — which may indicate a coordinated attack. Which AWS services implement this alert?

options.text: AWS Config rules checking Guardrail configurations every 5 minutes
CloudWatch Alarm on the InvocationIntervened metric (from Bedrock Guardrails) with a threshold of 100 in 5 minutes, sending an SNS notification
Amazon Macie scanning S3 logs every 5 minutes
AWS Trusted Advisor checking Guardrail utilisation

explanation: Bedrock Guardrails emits the InvocationIntervened CloudWatch metric for every intervention. A CloudWatch Alarm with a Sum threshold of 100 over a 5-minute period will trigger an SNS notification when the threshold is exceeded — providing real-time attack detection. Config monitors resource configurations. Macie scans S3 data content. Trusted Advisor provides best-practice recommendations, not real-time operational alarms.
source_topic: CloudWatch Alarm on InvocationIntervened for attack detection

question_text: An organisation has a written AI policy stating 'no financial advice, no competitor comparisons, no political content'. A governance engineer must translate these written policies into enforceable technical controls in Bedrock. What is the DIRECT translation mechanism?

options.text: Include the policies in the model's system prompt as instructions
Map each policy statement to a Bedrock Guardrails denied topic configuration with a natural language description
Add the policies to the company wiki and train developers to follow them
Apply SageMaker Model Cards to document the policy restrictions

explanation: Bedrock Guardrails Denied Topics is the direct, programmatic translation of written AI policies into enforceable technical controls. Each policy statement ('no financial advice') becomes a denied topic with a natural language description — the Guardrail then blocks any FM response on that topic, regardless of how the user phrases the request. System prompt instructions can be bypassed. Wiki + training relies on human compliance. Model Cards document restrictions but don't enforce them.
source_topic: Translating AI policy to Bedrock Guardrails denied topics

question_text: A company uses SageMaker to train models on datasets sourced from multiple S3 buckets and data sources. After a model quality incident, they need to trace back to the exact training dataset version, preprocessing job, and data source that produced the affected model. Which SageMaker feature enables this?

options.text: SageMaker Experiments — tracks training run metrics
SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking — automatically records artifact provenance across training jobs
AWS CloudTrail — records SageMaker API calls
Amazon S3 versioning — tracks changes to training data files

explanation: SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking automatically creates and maintains a provenance graph linking models back to their training jobs, processing jobs, datasets, and source data — enabling complete root-cause tracing for model quality incidents. SageMaker Experiments tracks metrics per run but not cross-artifact relationships. CloudTrail records API calls but not the ML artifact dependency graph. S3 versioning tracks file changes but not the downstream model dependencies.
source_topic: SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking for training incident root-cause analysis
